articles.title: Shingles cases dropping among people who got chickenpox vaccine, data shows
articles.summary: Shingles is dropping among people who got chickenpox shots but mysteriously rising in people 35 and older, new research shows.
articles.body: The chickenpox vaccine appears to protect against shingles, according to a large new analysis. Anyone who got infected with chickenpox as a child is at risk of later developing shingles, a painful, blistering rash that usually appears on one side of the body. For unknown reasons, cases of shingles have been gradually rising, even among younger adults, research has shown. However, new data suggests that a steep decline in chickenpox cases over the last three decades, thanks to the chickenpox vaccine, may contribute to a decline in shingles in the coming years. New data suggests that people ages 34 and younger may be less likely to develop shingles than previous generations. That’s because they are more likely to have been vaccinated against the varicella zoster virus, or chickenpox, which can reactivate years later as shingles. “Our data suggest that trend is now reversing in the very youngest adults, the first generation eligible to be vaccinated against chickenpox as children,” said registered nurse Kersten Bartelt, lead author of the report from Epic Research, which conducts research on health trends. Epic researchers used electronic health data from more than 85 million patients seen by healthcare providers in the United States. They logged shingles diagnoses between 2019 and 2026 and how many cases occurred in different age groups. The report, which was released Friday, found: Shingles cases dropped from 10.8 to 7.3 per 10,000 people for women ages 30 to 34 between 2019 and 2026, and fell from 11 to 7.3 for men in the same age group. Among 25- to 29-year-olds, rates of shingles cases more than halved, from 7.7 per 10,000 women and 7.5 per 10,000 men in 2019 to 3.2 and 3.0, respectively.In 18- to 24-year-olds, shingles dropped from 2.9 to 1.6 per 10,000 women and from 2.7 to 2.4 per 10,000 men. It’s a promising development, though because shingles is typically rare in people younger than 50, the data can’t prove whether the protection will last as they age, Bertelt said. Still, the new data suggests potential lifelong benefits of chickenpox vaccination. The Food and Drug Administration approved the first chickenpox vaccine in 1995, when it was added to the childhood vaccination schedule. In 1997, states began requiring it for school and daycare. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention currently recommends two doses of the varicella vaccine for children from ages 1 to 6. Since then, infections have plummeted by 97%, according to the CDC. A type of herpes virus that once killed as many as 150 children a year, chickenpox has been virtually wiped out by vaccination, experts say. “People who have had the chickenpox virus have a higher risk of developing shingles,” said Dr. Sharon Curhan, a physician and epidemiologist at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School in Boston, who was not involved in the study. “People who got the vaccine, while they could get shingles, are at much lower risk.” Why is shingles increasing among millennials? The Epic data also showed that rates of shingles are rising among people 35 and over, who are more likely to have had the chickenpox infection as children. There’s no clear evidence for what’s causing the rise in this group, but, ironically, it could be linked to the near elimination of the varicella zoster virus, experts say. “Before the vaccine was available, parents in their 20s, 30s, 40s, and grandparents, were exposed to younger children with chickenpox, so that was like a booster for them,” Curhan said. Other potential causes are higher rates of chronic stress, depression and anxiety, as well as autoimmune diseases, which weaken the immune system, Curhan said. Both shingles and chickenpox usually clear up on their own within a couple of weeks, although the virus that causes both infections can cause serious complications, said Dr. Anne Gershon, a professor emeritus of pediatrics at Columbia University medical school, who was not involved in the research. The most common is severe long-term nerve pain, a condition called postherpetic neuralgia. If a shingles outbreak occurs close to the eye, it can cause blindness, Bartelt said. Shingles infections have also been linked to a 20% higher risk of cognitive decline — potentially because the virus can reactivate in the head rather than cause a skin rash, said Gershon — as well as increased risk of stroke and heart disease.

articles.title: This amount of deli meat associated with higher dementia risk in compelling new review
articles.summary: A major review links just two daily slices of deli meat to a 44% higher dementia risk, raising questions about ultra-processed foods and brain health. Experts weigh in.
articles.body: Eating just two slices of deli meat a day was associated with a substantially higher risk of dementia, according to a new review of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) and brain health. The findings, published in the August 2026 issue of Annual Review of Nutrition, looked at dozens of human and animal studies, including one involving nearly 500,000 people in the U.K. The study found that each additional 25 grams of processed meat eaten daily corresponded with a 44% higher risk of all-cause dementia and a 52% higher risk of Alzheimer's. Twenty-five grams of processed meat equals roughly one to two slices of deli meat, depending on how thick the meat is sliced. JUST ONE SMALL SERVING OF ULTRA-PROCESSED FOOD A DAY LINKED TO HIGHER DISEASE RISK, MAJOR STUDY FINDS The review, done by an international team of 27 researchers, looked more broadly at whether diets high in UPFs may contribute to brain aging over time. UPFs include sugary drinks, packaged snacks and other heavily industrially processed foods that often contain ingredients such as emulsifiers, preservatives and artificial colors. "The main takeaway for consumers is that it is very easy to get food items into the food supply without really understanding what kinds of effects they have on health, including the health of the brain," lead author Owen Carmichael, Ph.D., of the Pennington Biomedical Research Center in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, told Fox News Digital. Some UPFs are so highly engineered that they "look like pharmaceuticals," Carmichael said. 5 ULTRA-PROCESSED FOODS THAT MAY BE WORSE FOR YOUR HEALTH THAN YOU THINK, EXPERT SAYS "Yet they don't face anywhere near the scrutiny pharmaceuticals face when trying to get on the market," he added. "When it comes to food safety, we sort of shoot first and ask questions later." Carmichael said researchers are investigating two leading theories on why UPFs are linked to brain health. One is that UPFs can damage heart and blood vessel health, indirectly affecting the brain. "Healthy heart, healthy mind," he said. In general, he said UPFs are "especially bad for your health from the neck down, damaging the heart, blood vessels, muscle, fat [and] liver." The other theory is that certain food additives may disrupt brain chemistry. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Both theories need further research, Carmichael said. Much of the current research still comes from animal studies, according to the review, and long-term randomized clinical trials are still lacking. The authors emphasized that the findings are observational and cannot prove that processed meat, which includes deli turkey, ham, salami, bacon, hot dogs and sausages, directly causes dementia. But for people looking to improve long-term brain health, Carmichael's "healthy heart, healthy mind" rule still applies. Ultra-processed foods make up about 55% of Americans’ daily calories, experts say. Many dietary recommendations overlap with long-standing heart-health advice, such as eating more fruits, vegetables and fish. The review cited research suggesting that replacing just 10% of calories from UPFs with unprocessed foods could lower dementia risk by 19%. Ultra-processed foods make up about 55% of Americans’ daily calories, experts note. UPFs tend to be inexpensive, convenient and heavily marketed — making them easy for many people to consume regularly, Dr. William Scott Burgin, a vascular neurologist at the University of South Florida and chief medical officer for NeuroEM Therapeutics, told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "UPFs are probably the worst for brain health," said Burgin, who was not involved with the new research. But he cautioned against lumping all UPFs together. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES "There are foods that get technically classified as ultra-processed, but are more likely neutral or may even be good for you, such as fortified whole grain cereals, dairy-based foods like yogurt, and packaged breads and grain products." Burgin also noted that most of the evidence comes from observational studies rather than research assigning people to specific diets. "All that being said, while I encourage people to reduce their consumption of UPFs, a cookie every now and then is not a problem," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He also encouraged a diet rich in omega-3s, antioxidants and polyphenols, while noting that some evidence also supports supplements such as B vitamins. Fox News Digital reached out to The Meat Institute, headquartered in Virginia, and The American Association of Meat Processors, based in Pennsylvania, for comment.

articles.title: Men are hiding potentially deadly disorder amid pressure to build the 'perfect' body
articles.summary: Sylvester Stallone's bulimia revelation spotlights a crisis experts say is surging among men and boys driven by looksmaxxing and musculature ideals.
articles.body: Days after Sylvester Stallone revealed his own history with bulimia, experts are highlighting a growing but often overlooked rise in eating disorders among men. The Academy Award-nominated actor, 80, revealed during an interview with The New York Times that he developed an "obsession" with eating habits while prepping for his role in the 1982 movie "Rambo." Stallone said he took pains to appear more "animalistic," drawing inspiration from jaguars and cats. "It became an obsession. Really bad. It got to the point where I became bulimic," he said during the interview. SYLVESTER STALLONE REVEALS SURPRISING HEALTH STRUGGLE BEHIND HIS FAMOUSLY RIPPED PHYSIQUE Bulimia nervosa is an eating disorder marked by episodes of binge-eating — consuming a large amount of food while feeling a loss of control — followed by purging behaviors such as vomiting, excessive use of laxatives or diuretics, fasting or excessive exercise, according to the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH). Brian Pollack, a licensed clinical social worker and certified eating disorders specialist at Hilltop Behavioral Health in Summit, New Jersey, specializes in treating males who struggle with eating disorders, which he said is "highly underreported." According to the National Association of Anorexia Nervosa and Associated Disorders (ANAD), about 30 million Americans experience an eating disorder during their lifetime, and roughly one-third are male. What's driving the trend? "Guys with eating disorders just present differently — for some men, it's about musculature … they continue to build muscle because they are afraid that they are weak, they want their muscles to align," Pollack told Fox News Digital. "We also see people who want to be so lean and pencil-thin that they don't eat whatsoever." The expert, who has not treated Stallone, compared today's body-image pressures on boys and men with the beauty ideals many girls and women faced during earlier decades. MEN FACE NEW PRESSURE TO STAY ‘HOT’ AS THEY AGE — AND IT’S NOT JUST ABOUT LIVING LONGER "We’re seeing this extreme need for perfection and musculature — and that is leading to bulimia right now," he told Fox News Digital. "It’s particularly in our adolescent boys, who are consuming a lot of information about the ideal of masculinity in the eyes of society at large." Societal expectations of masculinity can make it harder for men to identify and express feelings of vulnerability or distress, according to Pollack. "Bulimia, especially, is about control," he said. "And what is it that men want? They want to be in control on a superficial level." With binging, there is a loss of control over food — and purging is a way to get back in control, Pollack noted. COMMON GYM SUPPLEMENT COULD HELP FIGHT DEPRESSION, NEW RESEARCH SUGGESTS The increase in bulimia and other eating disorders among men may also be driven by a desire to emulate celebrities. "There's a big trend right now called ‘looksmaxxing,' where boys are harming themselves in pursuit of an ideal appearance, including undergoing cosmetic procedures to alter their jawlines," Pollack said. "It’s getting very scary out there, actually." Warning signs For many men, it may not be easy for others to recognize that they are struggling with bulimia or other eating disorders, as the binging and purging behaviors are usually done in secret, Pollack said. "They're hidden," he said. "People are ashamed of them at times." One red flag, he said, is if a loved one begins purchasing increasing amounts of supplements, such as creatine, or performance-enhancing substances such as human growth hormone. People with eating disorders may exhibit compulsive behaviors around both exercise and eating, including working out for multiple hours every day and carefully calculating every aspect of their diet. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Some men become fixated on restrictive eating patterns, Pollack said, including following strict ketogenic diets, consuming excessive amounts of protein or eating only foods they consider "clean," such as organic, whole-food or non-GMO products. In some cases, the obsession becomes so extreme that men may avoid eating foods prepared elsewhere or outside their strict standards. Pollack said some people may have "cheat days" where they visit fast-food restaurants and eat as much as they can, in an attempt to satisfy an "intense urge" stoked by restriction. "They binge, and we often see people hiding in the bathroom within 45 minutes after meals." Another warning sign is escalating use of laxatives or diuretics, with some people taking increasingly large amounts because smaller doses no longer produce the desired effect of feeling "emptied" or "in control." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Pollack emphasized that bulimia and other disorders are experienced among men at all ages, from middle school and high school through college and adulthood. "This is real, and men are afraid to talk about it," he said. "There's a real issue." The expert said men often don't have the vocabulary to talk about emotional distress, making eating disorders harder to identify. Instead, Pollack recommended asking questions about body goals — such as whether someone is trying to "sculpt your body" or "make sure that you have a six-pack" — and whether those pursuits are helping them avoid confronting difficult emotions. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Health effects Bulimia is known to have life-threatening health impacts. "Just on a baseline level, with someone who purges, we see electrolyte imbalances, along with kidney and liver damage," Pollack said. The expert shared that he has seen people go into cardiac arrest because prolonged malnutrition and repeated purging had severely damaged their hearts. Bulimia patients may face expensive dental work, he added, due to severe erosion of their tooth enamel. Esophagus issues, such as acid reflux and GERD, may also develop due to purging. "It's a very serious scenario."

articles.title: The 4 Biggest Red Flags to Look for in Your Family Medical History
articles.summary: In TODAY.com’s Expert Tip of the Day, a physician explains what your family’s medical history can reveal about your own health, and which red flags to watch for.
articles.body: Your family’s medical history can hold many clues about your own health. It can also reveal your risk of developing certain diseases and change when you should start screenings. That’s why it’s important to know about all the diseases and conditions that run among your close relatives. You may know your grandmother had cancer, for example. But do you know what kind and which stage? Or her age when she was diagnosed? Those small details matter, says Dr. Akshay Syal, an internal medicine physician and NBC News medical contributor. Syal joined TODAY in a segment aired Oct. 2 to explain the top red flags in your family medical history, what these could mean for your health, and what information to share with your doctor. Expert Tip of The Day: Look Out for These 4 Red Flags in Your Family Medical History Once you compile your family’s health history, Syal recommends looking for these four red flags: Disease at a young ageMultiple relatives with the same diseaseCertain cancer patternsKnown genetic conditions “One of the biggest red flags is disease happening at an unusually young age,” says Syal. A heart attack at 45, for example, is very different from a heart attack at 85. The same goes for strokes, diabetes and cancers. If a family member is diagnosed with a disease much earlier than is typical, it could suggest an inherited component, says Syal. Also, pay attention to two or more family members on the same side of the family having the same disease or condition. The next red flag to look for is patterns in cancer diagnoses across your family, says Syal — for example, if multiple close relatives had breast, colorectal or uterine cancer. Finally, if you learn about any genetic conditions or gene mutations in your family, such as Lynch syndrome, tell your doctor. Why It Matters The goal is to garner information and identify patterns, which a doctor can help interpret — not to self-diagnose. “None of these red flags mean you’re guaranteed to develop a disease. They simply give us information that may help us identify risk earlier and decide whether screening or prevention should change,” says Syal. A doctor may recommend you start getting colonoscopies or mammograms earlier and more frequently than average-risk individuals, for example. “It can also help us focus on prevention, (monitoring) things like blood pressure, cholesterol or other risk factors before a problem develops,” says Syal. Certain cancer patterns or gene mutations in your family could raise the risk of an inherited condition, and it may be suggested you pursue genetic counseling or testing. How to Get Started In order to compile your family’s medical history, first make a family tree, starting with your closest biological relatives and expanding out to both sides of the family: Parents and siblingsGrandparentsAunts and unclesNieces and nephews Next, fill in the blanks. Write down every known disease, major health condition or cause of death for each relative. Always note the details: the type, stage and age of diagnosis. If you don’t know, ask your family. (The holidays are coming up!) Write everything down so you don’t forget. Once you have your family medical history, share it with your doctor. Ask whether your history may increase your risk of any diseases and whether it could impact screenings or testing. Not everyone knows their biological family or has access to their health records. “If that’s you, don’t panic. Just tell the doctor everything you do know,” Syal notes. “Family history isn’t destiny, but knowing it gives you and your doctor an opportunity to be proactive,” he adds. TODAY’s Expert Tip of the Day series is all about simple strategies to make life a little easier. Every Monday through Friday, different qualified experts share their best advice on diet, fitness, heart health, mental wellness and more.

articles.title: Brooke Eby, Who Chronicled Life With ALS With Humor and Honesty, Dies at 37
articles.summary: Brooke Eby has died at 37. The ALS advocate inspired millions with candid, funny videos documenting life with the disease.
articles.body: Brooke Eby, who transformed her diagnosis with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis into one of social media’s most compelling chronicles of resilience, humor and advocacy, helping change how millions of people understood a devastating disease, has died. She was 37. The cause was complications of ALS, also known as Lou Gehrig’s disease, according to the ALS Network. When Eby was diagnosed in 2022 at age 33 after years of unexplained symptoms, she faced a prognosis that people with the disease know all too well: ALS is a fatal, progressive neurodegenerative disease with no cure and few effective treatments. Rather than retreat from public life, she leaned into it. Her videos, often equal parts comedy routine and medical diary, documented the realities of losing mobility without surrendering her personality. She joked about wheelchairs, dating, awkward encounters with strangers and the absurdities of living with a terminal illness, drawing millions of viewers who found themselves laughing before they learned something about ALS. In a 2023 appearance on TODAY, Eby described her philosophy succinctly. “Levity is my superpower,” she told Savannah Guthrie. “It’s really how I’m bringing my story to the world. I’m trying to use humor and really let ALS be heard.” Her advocacy extended beyond awareness. Speaking on the Brain & Life podcast, she challenged scientists, policymakers and donors to “operate at the speed of ALS,” arguing that a disease measured in months demanded research that moved with equal urgency. Working with the adaptive clothing company Silverts, she helped create the B.E. Collection, a line of stylish adaptive clothing designed for younger people with disabilities who often found existing options too clinical or geared toward older adults. A portion of the proceeds benefit Team Gleason, which supports people living with ALS. Unlike many public advocates who emerged after years of activism, Eby entered the spotlight almost accidentally. Two months after her diagnosis, she began writing down the funny moments of her new reality. Her first TikTok introduced audiences to a young woman determined to make people laugh before asking them to confront uncomfortable truths about terminal illness. What began as a handful of videos grew into one of the largest online communities devoted to ALS. “I always say my North Star was giving a face to ALS,” she said on the Brain & Life podcast. “Then one of my friends said, ‘Doesn’t it help you too?’ I had never even thought about it like that.” Born on Dec. 22, 1988, Eby grew up in Maryland and later worked in the technology industry at Salesforce. At 29, while living in New York City, she noticed she could no longer push off properly with her left foot while walking. Doctors initially suspected more common explanations. Over several years she underwent repeated testing before receiving an ALS diagnosis. Eby often described the emotional aftermath without embellishment. “I remember crawling into bed with a bag of M&M’s, party size,” she recalled during her appearance on TODAY. “It was just survival.” A turning point came at a friend’s wedding, where she arrived using a walker identical to the bride’s grandmother’s. Mortified, she considered leaving early until a friend suggested embracing the moment instead. Soon the bride was limboing beneath her walker and guests were taking “walker rides” across the dance floor. That evening, she later said, taught her that humor could dissolve discomfort more effectively than silence. As her disease progressed, from leg braces to a cane, then a walker and ultimately a wheelchair within months, she adapted rather than withdrew. She traded workout classes for reading, advocacy, speaking engagements and content creation, documenting not only her physical decline but the unexpected expansion of her emotional world. “When I got diagnosed,” she said on TODAY, “the future — that runway— was just cut off.” Yet she often insisted the disease had sharpened rather than diminished her appreciation for life. “I’m aware of more of the beauty and kindness in the world now than I was.” In interviews, she resisted being described as inspirational simply because she was living with a terminal illness. What she wanted, she said, was attention directed toward the disease. “There are two things that I would ask of people,” Eby told Savannah. “ALS research needs money… and follow my story. I think we associate ALS with characters who don’t look like me.”
